The French language version of this Document d'Enregistrement Universel (Universal Registration Document) was filed on
March 26, 2026 with the Autorité des Marchés Financiers (AMF), as competent authority under Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, without prior
approval pursuant to Article 9 of said regulation.
This Universal Registration Document may be used for the purposes of an offer to the public of securities or admission of securities to
trading on a regulated market if completed by a securities note and, if applicable, a summary and any amendments to the Universal
Registration Document. The whole is approved by the AMF in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/1129.

This Universal Registration Document, including the annual financial report, is a reproduction of the official version which has been
prepared in ESEF format and is available on the issuer’s website, www.carrefour.com.

     1.1.7        OUR RAISON D’ÊTRE

     At the Shareholders’ Meeting of June 14, 2019, the Group adopted a raison d’être, a statement enshrined in its Articles of Association
     that reasserts its commitment to leading the food transition for all by promoting healthier, more affordable food, while supporting the
     agricultural transition and helping to preserve the planet’s resources:

     “Our mission is to provide our customers with quality services, products and food accessible to all across all distribution channels.
     Thanks to the competence of our employees, to our broad territorial presence and to our ability to adapt to sustainable production and
     consumption modes, our ambition is to be the leader of the food transition for all.”

                                                                                       Alexandre Bompard, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer

                                                                                                                                                 4
  "Carrefour 2030": a new strategic plan focused on growth and value creation, prioritising
  customers, stores and technology
  Going forward, Carrefour is embarking on a new phase of growth and value creation with its new strategic plan "Carrefour 2030",
  focused on three core countries - France, Spain and Brazil - and on three priorities: winning over customers by leveraging price,
  freshness, loyalty and own brands; consolidating store growth through expansion and franchising; and accelerating performance
  through AI, tech and data.

  (i)   Win on product offering and customers
                                                                                                                                                 5
  To win and retain customers, Carrefour places price, fresh food, the Club, choice, and its own brands at the centre of its strategy.

  The Group is committed to maintaining its price leadership in Spain and Brazil, and to improving its price competitiveness in
  France year after year. To implement its price policy, Carrefour intends to leverage the purchasing gains generated by the
  Concordis European buying alliance, which aims for European co‑leadership among FMCG buying groups by 2030. Carrefour also
  plans to increase the number of Club customers to 60 million by 2030, up from 50 million in 2025, mainly through the launch of
  Nosso Clube in Brazil.
  Carrefour intends to differentiate itself on fresh products, the primary store traffic driver, with the ambition of reaching a 50%
                                                                                                                                                 6
  penetration rate in fruit and vegetables by 2030 (vs. 41% in 2025), building on alliances with recognised specialists, such as
  Marché Frais and the Blachère group, and the launch of new concepts.

  Carrefour will continue to develop its own brands 1.5 times faster than national brands and aims to launch Bulnez in Brazil, a new
  discount own‑brand with 500 product references at Atacadão by 2028, to meet the challenges of purchasing power.

  Carrefour is also stepping up its commitment to the food and climate transition. The Group pledges that by 2030, 50% of its food
  sales will come from products that contribute to a more balanced diet, and has become the world’s first retailer to announce the
  absence of the main ultra‑processed ingredients in its own brands. To address the climate, Carrefour is fast‑tracking the                      7
  decarbonisation of its activities and is ensuring that its 150 largest suppliers adopt a 1.5°C climate pathway by 2030.

       (ii) Consolidate growth from stores
       Carrefour aims to open 1,000 additional convenience stores in France and 750 in Spain for a total of 7,500 in the two countries,
       50 new Market stores in France, and 70 additional Atacadão stores in Brazil. The Match network will grow to 160 stores by 2030.

       The Group is stepping up its transformation towards a more asset‑light and entrepreneurial model: in France, 40 Market
       supermarkets will be converted into franchises each year. In hypermarkets, Carrefour continues to ramp up transfers to lease
       management for stores in need of revitalisation (15 such transfers in 2026).

       To ensure the commercial modernisation of hypermarkets in France, Carrefour will invest nearly 200 million euros a year.
       Between 5% and 10% of sales space on average will be reallocated from underperforming categories to growth verticals (including
       home, pet care, drugstore/beauty and leisure) and to fresh produce.

       (iii) Accelerate performance through AI, Tech, and Data
       Carrefour is positioning itself at the forefront of technology to transform its operations and create new revenue streams.

       The Group will invest 100 million euros a year in AI and roll out the Vusion platform across all its French hypermarkets and
       supermarkets to optimise shelf management and online order preparation.

       Carrefour became the first French food retailer in Europe to join Google's Universal Commerce Protocol. This partnership will
       enable customers to shop directly via AI agents (Gemini), radically simplifying the shopping experience.

       Taking full advantage of its data, the Group aims to double the sales of its Retail Media joint venture (Unlimitail) by 2028.

       (iv) Financial ambitions and capital allocation
       Carrefour is targeting an operating margin of 3.2% in 2028 and 3.5% in 2030 and cumulative net free cash flow of 5 billion euros
       between 2026 and 2028, with net free cash flow growing steadily each year.

       Carrefour intends to maintain an attractive shareholder return policy.

       The ordinary dividend will be based on a payout ratio of between 50% and 60% of adjusted (1) earnings per share starting in 2026.
       This dividend is set to grow steadily each year, based on adjusted earnings per share expected to grow in the high single‑digit
       range.

       Each year, the Board of Directors will decide on additional shareholder returns, taking account of the Group's financial position
       and outlook.

     performance and governance.

     Below are the changes to the CSR index from 2026 onwards. These changes make it possible to renew or close the KPIs expiring in
     2025 and to integrate new strategic CSR challenges, linked in particular to health, but also to downstream transportation and the
     adaptation of stores and agricultural sectors to climate change. Societal innovation, the use of data and artificial intelligence all
     contribute to achieving these objectives.

     (1) Food and non‑food.

         transportation by 2030. 10% reduction in virgin plastic in single‑use packaging for Carrefour brands by 2030 (vs. 2024).
     (3) 50% of food sales from products that contribute to a more balanced diet by 2030: objective based on the recommendations of France's national
         nutrition and health program (Programme National Nutrition Santé). This objective excludes Nutriscore D and E products, which should be

         tonnes of salt from Carrefour‑branded products by 2026 (vs. 2022).

         reduction of plastic use, biodiversity, animal welfare, etc.
     (5) Women to account for 50% of new cohorts of Graduate and Leaders School, 42% of managers (France only) and 35% of Top 200 Managers by
         2030.
     (6) These five key actions are to: (i) raise awareness of disability issues among 100% of employees, (ii) train 100% of managers on how to welcome a
         person with a disability into their teams, (iii) appoint Disability Advisors across all Group retail formats and countries, (iv) create an employee
         community focused on disability issues in each country, (v) launch three disability initiatives per year.

ensure the safety of people (customers, employees and service                ■ identifying and hierarchising risks and sites;

objectives are to ensure business continuity and to make                     ■ drawing    up a roadmap comprising action plans and related

                                                                                                                                                     1
  Description of the pilot project in France

  Carrefour's France Security department is in charge of the work on flooding risks.

  Step 1: mapping vulnerability levels

  1.   Risk map drawn up of Carrefour’s sites in France based on the French government's Flood Risk Prevention Plans (PPRI), the
       history of flooding in the region where the site is located and records of any flooding that has occurred in the past at the
       sites. The France Security department conducted its own risk assessment, which was cross‑checked with the assessments
       carried out by the Group's Insurance department, with the assistance of its insurance provider.
                                                                                                                                                     2
  2.   On‑site validation of vulnerability levels: one‑day audits were performed at the priority sites by a specialist consultancy firm
       accompanied by surveyors. The findings of these audits highlighted the need to adjust the recommendations.
  Step 2: Action plan

  1.   On‑site equipment: the on‑site audits identified improvements that needed to be made to all the sites to safeguard them
       against flooding, such as sealing openings with anti‑flooding devices and raising technical equipment above flood level. A
       national list of approved suppliers has been drawn up so that each store can purchase the equipment it needs under the best
       terms and conditions. Additional solutions may be put in place on a case‑by‑case basis to address the specific risks at each
                                                                                                                                                     3
       site.

  2.   On‑site team training: a risk and incident management guide has been drawn up, which also contains a section to be filled
       out by each site for identifying and listing specific risks. Training is delivered by a service provider to the safety and security
       teams at the highest‑risk sites.

      Carrefour has analysed its impact on water using the SBTN methodology, cross‑referencing different types of data to prioritise areas at
      risk. The analysis integrated the location of pressures from the Group’s activities, notably through water consumption data linked to raw
      materials, with the level of ecological vulnerability assessed through water stress indicators. This cross‑referencing made it possible to
      identify the regions most at risk of water resource depletion and to assign them a priority level for action. This work was carried out on
      the 15 priority raw materials defined by Carrefour when it first measured its biodiversity footprint in 2021, covering all its activities and its
      entire value chain. For more details on the work carried out through the SBTN on biodiversity, including pressure on water, see
      Section 2.1.2.4 Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4).

                        Plastic-related risks identified by Carrefour
                        Products sold make up for an estimated 90% of the plastic manufactured and used as part
                        of the Group’s activities, and 80% of this plastic comes from packaging.
                        The main impacts linked to the manufacture of plastics include soil and water pollution during oil extraction
                        and energy consumption and GHG emissions during its transformation into plastic as well as polluting
                        emissions in the air.



                        End-of-life plastics
                        When it comes to end-of-life plastics, processing and recycling capacities in the countries
                        in which the Group operates and the quantity of plastic involved in each country deter-
                        mine the risks. An estimated 20% of the plastic manufactured and used throughout the
                        value chain is recycled, 38% is incinerated, 56% is sent to landfi lls, and 6% is uncollected.
                        Indeed, the recycling rate of plastic, especially plastic not derived from household waste,
                        varies from country to country, from 1% in Brazil to 26% in France and 47% in Spain. These
                        three priority countries for the Group together represent more than 3/4 of the volume of
                        France and 47% in Spain. These three priority countries for the Group together represent
                        more than 3/4 of the volume of plastics produced.
                        The main impacts related to end-of-life plastics include air pollution and GHG emissions when the end-of-life
                        plastic is incinerated at the end of its life or soil and water pollution in the event of burial or discharge into nature.


                        Released microplastics
                        Microplastics can be released at different stages of the value chain. They can be released
                        into the air due to the use of vehicles for the transport of goods or the movement of
                        visitors. They can also be released into the water, for example through the washing of
                        clothes.
                        The main impacts linked to the release of microplastics include air, soil, and water pollution.


                        Migration of toxic substances
                        Prolonged interaction of plastics with liquid or moist food products may result in the
                        migration of sensitive substances into the food, particularly in connection with the
                        presence of additives. Rare non-food products may present the same risk of transfer.
                        The main impacts related to migration of toxic substances include adverse effects on human heath through the
                        migration of toxic substances from plastic packaging into food.

      Explanatory notes for Template 1:
      (1)   (N): (N) Indicates the financial year that the reported data refer to. Columns (2) to (14) pertain to financial year (N).(N‑1) Indicates the previous financial year. If no data
            were reported for financial year N‑1, leave columns (15) and (16) empty.
      (2)   Column (2) shall contain the denominator of the respective KPI.
      (3)   Column (3) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI that is associated with total Taxonomy‑eligible economic activities regardless of
            whether those activities are taxonomy‑aligned or not.
      (4) Column (5) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI that is associated with total Taxonomy‑aligned economic activities.
      (5)   Columns (6) to (11) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI that is associated with Taxonomy‑aligned economic activities that contribute
            substantially to the respective environmental objective. For the respective KPI, the sum of the proportions in columns (6) to (11) shall be equal to the figure in the column
            (5).
      (6) Column (12) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI that is associated with Taxonomy‑aligned economic activities that are enabling
          economic activities.
      (7)   Column (13) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI that is associated with Taxonomy‑aligned economic activities that are transitional
            economic activities.
      (8) Column (14) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI associated with economic activities that are considered non‑material with respect to
          the respective KPI and not assessed for Taxonomy‑eligibility and Taxonomy‑alignment in accordance with Article 2(1a), (1b), and (1c), respectively. For an economic
          activity considered material with respect to a KPI (turnover, CapEx, or OpEx), undertakings shall assess the Taxonomy‑eligibility and alignment of that KPI pertaining to
          that activity in its entirety and not consider portion of that KPI pertaining to that activity as non‑material. Column (14) shall not include any portion of turnover, CapEx, or
          OpEx associated with material economic activities.
      (9) Column (16) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI, pertaining to the financial year (N‑1), that is associated with total Taxonomy‑aligned
          economic activities pertaining to the financial year (N‑1).
      (10) Columns (5) to (11) to avoid double counting: if the figure in column (5) contains Taxonomy‑aligned economic activities that contribute substantially to more than one
           environmental objective at the same time, the substantial contribution of those economic activities to multiple environmental objectives should be indicated under the
           respective environmental objectives in columns (6) to (11) of Template 2 on respective activity rows, but should not be double counted in columns (5) to (11) of Template 1.

      Explanatory notes for Template 2:
      (1)   Non‑financial undertakings shall duplicate this template to disclose separately the turnover, the CapEx and the OpEx KPIs, clearly indicating in the title of each table which
            KPI the table refers to. Where non‑financial undertakings disclose zero Taxonomy‑eligible KPI (turnover, CapEx, or OpEx, respectively), in Template 1, column (3), they
            may omit disclosing Template 2 for that KPI.
      (2)   (N) indicates the financial year that the reported data refer to. Columns (2) to (14) pertain to financial year (N).
      (3)   For activity rows, column (2), the Code constitutes the abbreviation of the relevant objective to which the economic activity is eligible to make a substantial contribution,
            as well as the Section number of the activity in the relevant Annex covering the objective, i.e.:
            -    Climate Change Mitigation: CCM
            -    Climate Change Adaptation: CCA
            -    Water and Marine Resources: WTR
            -    Circular Economy: CE
            -    Pollution Prevention and Control: PPC
            -    Biodiversity and Ecosystems: BIO
            For example, the Activity "Afforestation" has the Code: CCM 1.1. Where activities are eligible to make a substantial contribution to more than one objective, the codes for
            all objectives should be indicated.
      (4) For activity rows, column (3) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI, as reported in Template 1, that is associated with a Taxonomy‑eligible
          economic activity regardless of whether or not that activity is Taxonomy‑aligned, or only a portion of that activity is Taxonomy‑aligned.
      (5)   For activity rows, column (5) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI, as reported in Template 1, that is associated with a Taxonomy‑aligned
            economic activity, or with the Taxonomy‑aligned portion of a Taxonomy‑eligible activity.
      (6) For activity rows, columns (6) to (11) shall contain the proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI, as reported in Template 1, that is associated with a
          Taxonomy‑aligned economic activity, or its portion, that contributes substantially to the respective environmental objective for which the economic activity is
          Taxonomy‑eligible. Columns corresponding to the environmental objectives for which the economic activity is not Taxonomy‑eligible should be left empty. Where a
          Taxonomy‑aligned economic activity, or its portion, contributes substantially to several environmental objectives, the columns under those environmental objectives shall
          contain the corresponding proportion of the denominator of the respective KPI, as reported in Template 1, that is associated with that activity or its portion. In other
          words, where an activity contributes substantially to more than one environmental objective at the same time, its substantial contribution should be indicated under
          multiple environmental objectives in the row pertaining to that economic activity.
      (7)   Column (14) shall contain the ratio of the figure in column (5) divided by the figure in column (3) in the respective rows.
      (8) Row “Sum of alignment per objective”: columns (6) to (11) shall contain the sum of figures for all reported activities under the respective columns. The sum of columns (6)
          to (11) on this row might possibly result in more than 100%.
      (9) Row “Total KPI”: columns (3) to (13) shall contain the sum of figures for all reported activities under the respective columns. For columns (4) to (11), when performing the
          summation in the row “Total KPI”, non‑financial undertakings shall not double count the contributions to multiple environmental objectives and include only the
          environmental objective they deem the most relevant. Figure in column (5) in this row, i.e., Total Taxonomy‑aligned KPI, shall equal the sum of figures reported in
          columns (6) to (11) in this row. The figures reported in the row “Total KPI” in columns (3) to (13) in Template 2 shall be equal to the figures reported in corresponding
          columns (3) to (13) in the Template 1. In order to avoid double counting, financial undertakings will take into account the Total KPI figure as reported in Template 1 when
          computing their own KPIs.

Assessing risks to facilitate prevention

To reduce the number and severity of work‑related accidents,                                                                                            7
Carrefour puts risk assessment and prevention at the heart of its
health and safety management system. A risk assessment
identified several objectives: the first is to maintain a high level of
physical, mental and social well‑being among employees; the
second is to prevent the risks to which employees are exposed in
the workplace and thus protect them from any harm; as well as
to keep employees in a job that is suited to their physical and
psychological abilities.

      2.2.3.1 Analysis of identified environmental risks

      Greenhouse gas emissions
      Definition: The company emits greenhouse gases (GHG) as part of its operations. These mainly include carbon dioxide (CO2),
      methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O) and fluorinated gases used in particular for refrigeration systems.

      UPSTREAM risks                                                      Risks relating to GROUP OPERATIONS
      GHG emissions associated with the production of goods and Leaks of refrigerant gases used in store cooling systems (air
      services (agricultural production, land‑use change and product conditioning, refrigeration units and cold storage rooms)
      processing)                                                    Excessive consumption of carbon‑based energy to run stores and
      GHG emissions from transporting goods (by rail, road and air)  warehouses
      Excessive energy use and leaks of refrigerants in the cold chain
      and in product production


      Consumption of marine resources and degradation of marine ecosystems
      Definition: Overexploitation of marine resources, degradation of the seabed and pollution of the seas and oceans can significantly
      impact marine habitats by depleting resources and degrading ecosystems. Food companies depend on marine ecosystems and their
      ecosystem services such as climate regulation, food production and raw materials.

      UPSTREAM risks
      Extracting, using and overexploiting marine resources for fishing
      Degradation of habitats through fishing techniques


      Waste and poor waste management
      Definition: Waste is defined as any substance or object that the undertaking holding said substance or object discards or intends or is
      required to discard (including food waste). Disposing of waste can have a negative impact on the environment and human health due
      to excessive exploitation of natural resources, pollution caused by non‑recyclable waste or poor waste management, food waste and
      greenhouse gas emissions.

      UPSTREAM risks                                                      Risks relating to GROUP OPERATIONS
      Excessive production and a lack of waste sorting in the agricultural Excessive production and a lack of waste sorting by warehouses,
      sector and in the processing of raw materials, products and stores or in property management/development (construction
      packaging                                                            and renovation)
      Food and non‑food waste in the production chain (waste of On‑site food and non‑food waste due to poor management of
      resources, products discarded on farms and in processing plants) inventories, promotions and unsold items
      Production of waste in the supply chain due to irregularities in the
      cold chain, poor management of inventories and deliveries,
      product withdrawals/recalls, etc.


      Deforestation and contribution to land‑use change
      Definition: Deforestation means reducing forest areas to free up land for other activities or to use forest resources directly. Land‑use
      change is, more broadly, the process of replacing one type of soil or vegetation to meet human needs such as farming or
      urbanisation. These two processes contribute significantly to climate change and biodiversity loss as natural habitats are destroyed.

      UPSTREAM issues
      Deforestation associated with the supply of sensitive raw materials (cocoa, palm oil, wood and paper, beef in Brazil, etc.)
      Indirect deforestation associated with the production of certain products, in particular animal products using soy for animal feed
      Conversion of ecosystems associated with the agricultural production of certain sensitive raw materials, in particular soy used for
      animal feed

Microplastic emissions
                                                                                                                                                  1
Definition: Microplastics refer to plastic particles generated or used during production processes. They may leave the undertaking's
installations in the form of emissions, products or parts of products or services. These microplastics can be produced unintentionally
when larger pieces of plastic, such as plastic waste or synthetic textiles, become worn, or they can be deliberately manufactured and
added to products for specific purposes.

UPSTREAM risks
Emission of microplastics during agricultural production or product processing (plastic sheeting, etc.)                                           2
Emission of microplastics by tyres during goods transport
Excessive use of plastics in the composition of products and packaging (textiles, etc.) which generates microplastics
Discarding polluting materials and substances into the ocean, in particular plastics used in product and package processing



Consumption of energy resources

Definition: Energy refers to all types of energy production and consumption, whether renewable (including biogas and biomass) or
non‑renewable. Excessive energy use and promotion of high‑carbon energy sources have a major impact on greenhouse gas                             3
emissions. Buying green energy – energy that comes solely from renewable sources (hydro, wind, solar, geothermal, etc.) – is a major
challenge in the energy transition.

polluting industrial processes)

      2.2.3.2 Analysis of identified human rights risks

      Inadequate working conditions
      Definition: Working conditions refer to all the factors that contribute to ensuring a just and fair working environment for each and
      every worker by promoting safety, physical and mental integrity and well‑being at work. Inadequate working conditions exist in various
      forms, such as working hours that are too long or not respected, an unsuitable working environment that puts workers' health and
      safety at risk, an insecure employment contract and a lack of work‑life balance.

      UPSTREAM risks
      Failure to respect well‑being at work, failure to provide good working conditions (hygienic premises and toilets and washing facilities,
      access to drinking water), poor work organisation (working hours, night work, impact of restructuring), work‑life imbalance, and
      risk of stress
      Insecure employment contracts and insufficient employee benefits (contract termination due to illness, disability, retirement or
      family commitments)
      Deteriorating work environment: unhealthy, arduous work, extreme temperatures, lack of ergonomics


      Child labour, forced labour and illegal work
      Definition: Forced labour corresponds to work performed under duress, including situations where individuals are forced to work
      through the use of violence, intimidation, manipulation linked to debt, confiscation of identity documents or threats of being reported
      to the immigration authorities, or by more subtle means. Illegal work is work carried out outside the law. It may include, for example,
      unpaid working hours, the absence of employment contracts, undeclared employees, contracts written in a language that is not
      understood, and the employment of undocumented foreign nationals. Finally, child labour refers to any economic or domestic activity
      carried out by a child of school age, which is harmful to his or her health, safety or physical, mental, social or moral development, and
      which prevents him or her from fully enjoying his or her right to education.

      UPSTREAM risks
      Forced or compulsory labour
      Withholding identity documents, threats against illegal immigrants
      Withholding or non‑payment of wages, debt bondage
      Unpaid working hours
      Lack of employment contracts, contracts in a language that is not understood
      Undeclared workers, work by undocumented foreign nationals
      Forced or undeclared apprenticeships
      Unlawfully paid or undeclared activities


      Failure to pay adequate wages
      Definition: Failure to pay a decent wage means: (1) failure to pay the minimum wage set by local regulations, (2) a deterioration in the
      living conditions of the worker and their family, particularly in terms of food, water, housing, education, health care, transport, clothing
      and other essential needs, including preparation for unforeseen events.

      UPSTREAM risks
      Poor living conditions for workers and their families
      Pay below the poverty line and/or the minimum wage, lack of benefits or bonuses for workers
      Poor distribution of value among the various players in the supply chain, particularly farmers and farm workers

Unequal treatment and discrimination
                                                                                                                                                        1
Definition: Unequal treatment refers to situations in which people are treated without dignity or respect, on grounds of race, skin
colour, religion, sex, sexual orientation, age, disability, political opinion, national or social origin, or any other personal characteristic.
This means that not all individuals enjoy the same rights and opportunities, and they are not all subject to the same rules and
conditions, which constitutes discrimination.

2.2.3.3 Analysis of identified health and safety risks

Occupational health and safety violations
Definition: Health and safety at work have a number of specific objectives, designed to protect employees. The first objective is to
maintain a high level of physical, mental and social well‑being among employees. The second challenge of occupational health is to                  4
prevent the risks to which employees are exposed in the workplace and accordingly protect them from harm. The final objective is to
keep employees in a job that is suited to their physiological and psychological abilities.

Consumer health and safety violations due to quality, compliance or product safety failure
Definition: The risk of harming consumer health due to product quality, compliance or safety issues as a result of the products not

marine resources – ● favour the most abundant species depending on the geography and the state of stocks: Carrefour can

      RISK                 PREVENTION AND MITIGATION MEASURES IN PLACE
                           The specific case of canned tuna:
                           The Carrefour group's quality manuals specify the rules applicable to Carrefour‑brand canned tuna. These rules
                           include the following:
                           ■ fishing techniques that are prohibited or promoted;
                           ■ species to favour depending on stocks;
                           ■ implementation of minimum fish sizes, etc.

                           These specific criteria, which were revised in 2024, are implemented through purchases made by the
                           international purchasing centre that covers four European countries, and are distributed to the other countries
                           for gradual application.
                           The Group's quality specifications and documentation provide for the following measures:
                           ■ prohibit the use of vessels on the IUU (Illegal, Unreported, Unregulated) fishing blacklists, suspected of illegal

                              activities, or flying the flag of a country subject to a yellow card from the European Union;
                           ■ require the use of vessels registered and authorised by fisheries management organisations (RFMOs);
                           ■ require that purse seiners have an IMO or UBI registration number from the competent authorities;
                           ■ mandatory membership of the ISSF's PVR programme (International Seafood Sustainability Foundation’s

                              ProActive Vessel Register), wherever possible;
                           ■ prohibit transshipment, unless it is supervised according to ISSF criteria;
                           ■ extensive traceability right down to the fishing vessel: the complete list of vessels authorised to supply the

                              Group is included in the specifications of each supplier. The Group thus verifies that the vessels are registered
                              in the ISS's PVR programme (ProActive Vessel Register of the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation)
                              and that they are not on the blacklists of IUU (Illegal, Unreported, Unregulated) fishing, suspected of illegal
                              activities or flying the flag of a country subject to an EU yellow card;
                           ■ prohibit at‑sea transshipment: this measure requires boats to disembark regularly at the port for registration/

                              port control and reduces the risk of slavery.
                           Also, to combat illegal fishing, Carrefour ensures that all purse seiners are covered by observers or cameras for
                           its own‑brand tuna products. Carrefour is also putting in place third‑party inspectors during unloading to verify
                           the accuracy of data recorded by onboard observers for its own‑brand tuna products caught without
                           fish‑aggregation devices (FADs).

                           ■ innovation with the Group’s suppliers to reduce unsold food: in particular thanks to the joint work of

                             such as optimising donations to charities or recovering biowaste;
                           ■ recovery of non‑food waste: in collaboration with its suppliers, Carrefour works to cut down the production

                             of waste packaging and point‑of‑sale advertising materials at each store. The Group promotes sorting and
                             recovery through innovative solutions such as joint collection rounds from different sorting systems, the
                             reduction of excess packaging through reuse, the pooling of new recycling and product reuse streams, and
                             the digitalisation of customer communications.

Deforestation and Carrefour has identified certain sensitive raw materials whose production can have a major impact on
contribution to   biodiversity: wood/paper, soy, beef, palm oil and cocoa. The Group is taking a number of measures to reduce
land‑use change – the risks associated with these materials:
upstream
                  ■ guaranteeing that these raw materials do not come from deforested areas, thanks to traceability and strict

                  PEFC for lower‑risk areas, and European ecolabel for best manufacturing practice.                                           3

                  ■ the French National Strategy to Combat Imported Deforestation (SNDI);

                  ■ the Soy Transparency Coalition and the Global Canopy's Forest 500.

                  Brazilian beef: implementation of a specific governance system with the creation of a high‑level Forest                     4
                  Committee, responsible for overseeing geomonitoring and territorial projects aimed at achieving a supply of
                  beef from areas at risk of deforestation. The Group applies a pre‑approval process for suppliers, based on a strict
                  set of rules; failure to comply with these rules may result in penalties or in the Group no longer using them as a
                  supplier. The farms supplying these abattoirs are assessed every week by an independent third party using
                  geospatial analysis to check that they comply with social and environmental criteria. In the event of
                  non‑compliance, operations are temporarily or permanently suspended until the situation is rectified.
                  Cocoa: drawing‑up of a commitment charter to promote sustainable sourcing. This charter contains
                  requirements to tackle deforestation and child labour, compensate growers more fairly, and related to
                  traceability and transparency in the supply chain. The charter is implemented through use of certifications,
                                                                                                                                              5
                  robust voluntary programmes put in place by suppliers, and the results of trader assessments conducted
                  through the Retailer Cocoa Collaboration. Carrefour is also a partner of the CEMOI Transparence Cacao
                  programme, which ensures complete traceability from the bean to the consumer and covers around 30
                  Carrefour‑brand chocolate bars, including eight organic bars. The programme helps fight deforestation while
                  improving the living and working conditions of cocoa farmers.

      Microplastic         Carrefour has conducted an analysis of the impacts of plastic directly related to Carrefour’s operations in key

Human rights
Inadequate working In accordance with Carrefour's purchasing rules, an initial social audit must be carried out for all supplier plants
conditions           located in high‑risk or at‑risk countries. The audits are conducted under Initiative for Compliance and
Child labour, forced Sustainability (ICS) and Business Social Compliance Initiative (BSCI) standards (1). The required rating is A or B (C,
labour and illegal   D and E ratings do not qualify).
work – upstream      For supply chains identified as at‑risk following a raw material and production process analysis, additional
                     guarantees are required and social audits are conducted. The audit process is as follows:                                      2
                     ■ a preliminary review during the audit: the local Sourcing teams responsible for procurement perform on‑site

                       checks to verify if the plant complies with basic social, environmental and quality requirements. This
                       inspection is the first key stage in the process;
                     ■ initial audit: an independent firm performs an unannounced social audit. If the plant complies sufficiently with

                       the ICS and BSCI standards, it may be added to the list of suppliers. A report and accompanying action plan
                       are issued systematically to correct any instances of non‑compliance or to make improvements to any
                       identified areas of weakness. If the audit findings contain an alert, i.e., a critical point of non‑compliance, the
                       supplier will not be added to the list. The alerts are defined by the ICS methodology and concern child labour
                       or forced labour. The findings of the initial audits are rechecked via additional audits – the frequency of which            3
                       varies from every few months up to no longer than every two years – for suppliers that represent the lowest
                       risks;
                     ■ follow‑up audit: once added to the list of suppliers, unannounced follow‑up audits are carried out periodically

                       and always by independent firms. These audits are performed at least every two years and may be more
                       frequent depending on the criticality of any non‑compliance issues identified during previous audits. Carrefour
                       teams monitor compliance and, in some cases, may inspect sites to assess compliance with action plans. If
                       the results of a follow‑up audit indicate non‑compliance, the supplier must take immediate corrective action.
                       An inspection is then carried out within a reasonable timeframe to ensure the corrective actions have been
                       taken. Action plans are thus systematically drawn up following an audit, adapted in line with the
                                                                                                                                                    4
                       non‑compliance issues encountered. If critical non‑compliance is not corrected, the supplier is delisted;
                     ■ specific audit/inspection: Carrefour may hire an external firm to check one‑off or specific items, as with the

                       Bangladesh Accord signed in 2013 by a coalition of international brands and the biggest trade unions to
                       promote fire safety and the safety of buildings in the country.

                           Special cases:
                           Environmental and human rights violations caused by cotton production: cotton from Uzbekistan and
                           Turkmenistan is banned by Group procedures. Carrefour created an organic cotton production chain in the
                           Madhya Pradesh region combining high‑quality organic cotton, decent pay for producers and traceability
                           starting from the seed. The Group aims to increase the proportion of organic cotton in its total supply, while
                           raising the standards for conventional cotton. Carrefour also applies blockchain technology to some of its TEX
                           BIO textile products. Using a QR code, consumers can access information that tracks the product pathway from
                           the organic cotton farm to the point of sale.
                           Human rights violations caused by textile production: local projects in high‑risk regions (own‑brand suppliers)
                           include:
                           ■ incorporating environmental requirements into the Good Factory Standard;
                           ■ a project with the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs (IPE) to assess the environmental performance

                             of production plants in China;
                           ■ the Clean Water Project in Asia to prevent or counteract industrial pollution risks.

                           Monthly screening of the supply chain is carried out using the Sentinel tool via social media/internet, etc.
                           Action plans for alerts in the Xinjiang region: the Carrefour group does not source any products directly in the
                           Xinjiang region. Carrefour nevertheless monitors its sourcing to ensure compliant working conditions for all
                           materials that may be produced in this region. In view of the risk of forced labour in the cotton supply chain,
                           Carrefour requires all of its suppliers to be transparent about their supply chain and to be able to trace cotton
                           back to its origin. Any dubious reports are investigated by asking the supplier for:
                           ■ supporting documents for the transaction;
                           ■ contracts;
                           ■ certificates of origin to prove that the origin of the cotton is not prohibited.

                           Mapping of the Group's supply chain and alerts received from various channels have led to the identification of
                           eight additional sources with suspicious links to Xinjiang province. Alternatives have been found to replace
                           them. In 2022, a third party was hired to carry out checks of these suppliers’ warehouses and spinning mills to
                           verify the suppliers’ disclosures and carry out follow‑up monitoring procedures. Carrefour has launched spinning
                           mill inspections with its local teams, starting with key integrated suppliers.
                           Action plan relating to alerts in the Tamil Nadu region: collective work began in 2021 for this sourcing area in:
                           ■ classifying the Tamil Nadu region as "high‑risk" by local Global Sourcing teams in terms of social compliance

                             and factory/importer management;
                           ■ mapping the spinning mills of the area in the "Sustainability Map" platform of the Initiative for Compliance and

                             Sustainability (ICS) and evaluating their performance via an audit and a specific questionnaire, with priority
                             given to key suppliers;
                           ■ implementing a Worker Voice ethics hotline to ensure a whistleblowing facility at the local level. In 2022, the

                             Group rolled out an additional whistleblowing channel to give workers an opportunity to make reports
                             anonymously. The new whistleblowing line was initially made available in the mills of our main suppliers and it
                             can be extended to tier 1 suppliers if necessary. This practice, which goes beyond the scope of a social audit,
                             is intended to identify risks upstream and to implement systematic corrective measures.
                           For all production facilities in the Tamil Nadu region, issues related to social and environmental responsibility
                           should be managed by local Carrefour Global Sourcing teams. Moreover, since spinning mills are particularly
                           concerned by the problem, an Indian supplier whose garment factory is located outside Tamil Nadu but who
                           sources its yarn or material in Tamil Nadu must also be monitored by Carrefour's local Global Sourcing teams.
      Failure to pay   In relation to adequate wages, Carrefour’s purchasing rules include audits on compliance with the minimum
      adequate wages – wage, legal overtime pay requirements and freedom of association. The social performance of suppliers is
      upstream         regularly monitored and checked through social audits. Corrective action plans are systematically implemented
                       and progress monitored over time. In addition to social audits, Carrefour develops local projects to meet the
                       specific needs of its suppliers. More than 80% of cases of non‑compliance identified in plants in high‑risk
                       countries each year relate to one of the following three categories: "compensation, benefits and conditions",
                       "health and safety" and "working hours".
                       The Supplier Ethics Charter also stipulates that “The Supplier undertakes to grant its employees remuneration
                       that is equal to or more than the statutory minima or, failing which, to the relevant benchmark standards of the
                       sector of activity. In any case, this remuneration must be fair and adapted to local living conditions.”
                       Lastly, by signing the Charter, suppliers commit to ensuring that their affiliates or subcontractors comply with
                       these principles all along the supply chain as part of their business relationship with the Group.

Unequal treatment To prevent unequal treatment and discrimination, Carrefour:
and discrimination ■ requires its suppliers: to respect the principles of equal opportunity and non‑discrimination in employment,
– upstream
                     including on the grounds of gender, age, religion, ethnic origin, disability or any other characteristic protected         3
                     by law. These requirements are included in the Supplier Ethics Charter;
                   ■ applies international standards: such as the ILO non‑discrimination standards;
                   ■ carries out social and monitoring audits: and assesses discrimination and equal treatment practices in

                     factories, plantations and production sites. The audits cover recruitment, promotions, pay and working
                     conditions. In the event of non‑compliance, the supplier must take corrective steps within a specified
                     timeframe;
                   ■ uses certifications and labels: suppliers are encouraged to obtain social certifications that incorporate equal

                     opportunity and non‑discrimination criteria (SA8000 includes requirements on the fair treatment of workers
                     and non‑discrimination). Sustainable and fair trade labels sometimes include indicators for gender equality and            4
                     anti‑discrimination.
Unequal treatment Carrefour deploys the following tools in‑house to prevent unequal treatment and discrimination:
and discrimination ■ the Supplier Ethics Charter and Code of Conduct: Carrefour enforces the principle of equal treatment and
– operations
                     prohibits all forms of discrimination across all its sites and functions. The principles cover gender, age,
                     disability, religion, sexual orientation and any other characteristics protected by law;
                   ■ Diversity & Inclusion Policy: Carrefour has put in place a formal policy to promote diversity and inclusion

                     across all operations. The Group aims to ensure balanced representation, equal pay and fair access to
                     promotion and training;                                                                                                    5
                   ■ inclusive recruitment: with standardised processes to reduce bias and training for recruiters and managers.

                   ■ training and awareness‑raising: internal training programmes are offered to raise employees' awareness of

                   ■ mentoring and development: mentoring and professional development programmes are offered to

                     under‑represented groups to ensure equal access to opportunities.
                   The specific case of Brazil:
                   The Carrefour Brazil group does not tolerate any discriminatory practices, and all incidents of discrimination are           6
                   recorded and investigated and disciplinary measures taken against any persons who are proved to have been
                   involved, regardless of their position, function, type of contract or standing in the organisation, whether in
                   relations between employees or in their ecosystem as a whole.
                   The Group has launched a pilot project to guarantee in‑store security in the Porto Alegre region, involving a
                   review of the hiring model, training, protocols and management of these teams. Given the positive outcome of
                   this project, it has been extended to 109 other stores in Brazil. Moreover, 3,058 direct employees of the
                   Carrefour Brazil Group have received training on in‑store racism‑related issues.
                   The Carrefour Brazil Group has also teamed up with the Zumbi dos Palmares University to help create a training
                   programme in private security management. In addition to technical training, the programme also includes
                                                                                                                                                7
                   topics related to ethnic and race relations, human rights, alternative dispute resolution methods, crisis and risk
                   management. 90 Group employees benefited from this grant to attend the course.

      operations
                           Workplace Health and Safety management training programme has been set up for site managers, the Es@nté
                           tool promotes the occupational risk prevention approach and facilitates administrative management of
                           workplace accidents and occupational illnesses, and the Wittyfit tool focuses on psychosocial risk prevention.
                           Prevention of musculoskeletal disorders: massive investment in handling assistance equipment (automatic
                           pallet wrapping machines, stocking carts, etc.), in‑depth studies on workstation ergonomics, alterations to
                           furniture, and gym sessions to prepare employees before they start work.
                           Prevention of stress and psychosocial risks: stress management training, hotlines and free remote
                           psychological support, etc. In France, employees have toll‑free access to a support line.
      Consumer health      Carrefour implements a series of requirements and procedures to guarantee the quality and compliance of the
      and safety           products it sells. Carrefour's control plans also include consumer focus groups and warehouse and in‑store
      violations due to    checks of product freshness and origin.
      quality,
      compliance or        Crisis management, alert and product recall: to make sure that non‑compliant products cannot reach the end
      product safety       consumer, for example, online information platforms have been developed to help the relevant supplier provide
      failure              the data required for product recall. The platforms are also used to identify and warn the warehouses and stores
                           likely to have received batches of non‑compliant products, for more effective recall. As a further precaution, the
                           EAN barcode of recalled products is also blocked at checkout.
                           Carrefour has an alert system called AlertNet to inform all stores as quickly as possible if they must withdraw or
                           recall a product. The system is available online at all times and access is free for suppliers. In the event of an
                           alert, Carrefour immediately withdraws the products concerned. Verification of effective withdrawal is carried
                           out within 24 hours, and feedback on the quantity of products concerned follows within three working days of
                           the withdrawal order.
                           Monitoring plans for controlled products: controlled products are analysed for quality, performance and
                           compliance. Carrefour commissions independent laboratories to conduct analyses and, in some cases,
                           additional product tests to ensure compliance. To ensure that products meet consumer expectations, tests may
                           also be conducted with consumer panels or by experts. Monitoring commissioned by Carrefour complements
                           the supplier's self‑monitoring, with the primary aim of regularly verifying the compliance of Carrefour‑brand
                           products with applicable laws and specific provisions integrated into the contracts of controlled products.
                           Analysis takes many factors into account, including the identification of dangers and their characteristics,
                           exposure assessment, risk characterisation, control measures, degree of certainty, population sensitivity and
                           probability of occurrence.
                           Quality procedures and policies: Carrefour works to ensure the quality and safety of its own‑brand products in
                           all of the Group's host countries, operating a five‑pronged policy: supplier compliance with product quality
                           standards, product specifications, quality control plans and customer opinion surveys, in‑house expertise, and
                           traceability and data tracking.

      2.2.7      MONITORING SYSTEM FOR MEASURES IMPLEMENTED

      France’s duty of care law requires companies to set up a system to track the measures they have taken and assess their effectiveness.



      Qualitative          Qualitative monitoring of company measures is carried out regularly through interviews with the operational
      monitoring           business teams, informed by alerts reported via the various channels and an annual questionnaire sent to the
                           Group’s eight integrated countries.

      Quantitative         Carrefour has metrics in place on human health and safety, human rights and the environment. Collected using
      monitoring           the Group’s reporting tools, audits and other mechanisms, these metrics are used to assess the relevance and
                           effectiveness of Company measures.
                           See Section 2.2.5.2 Prevention and mitigation measures in place.

2.2.8.2 Main measures implemented in 2025

TYPES OF RISKS                  MEASURES IMPLEMENTED IN 2025
Risks of environmental damage
Contribution to climate change Carrefour is committed to reducing its emissions and decided to develop its climate transition plan
                               using ADEME's ACT Evaluation methodology. The results confirm that the target of a 32% reduction
                               in its GHG emissions by 2030 is in line with a 1.5°C pathway.
                                                                                                                                                   2
                                In 2025, Carrefour participated in the launch of the LESS (Low Emissions Sustainable Sourcing)
                                platform, which aims to reduce the carbon footprint of supply chains. This project was coordinated
                                by the Fédération du Commerce et la Distribution (FCD) and Perifem, and brings together the
                                following banners: Auchan, Carrefour, Coopérative U, Groupe Casino, Les Mousquetaires, Leclerc,
                                Lagardère Travel Retail, Lidl and Metro France.
Consumption of marine           In 2025, Carrefour organised a stakeholder panel on the canned tuna supply chain, bringing together
resources                       stakeholders with expertise in environmental issues, the protection of human rights and consumer
                                health.
                                                                                                                                                   3
Waste and poor waste            Carrefour has joined the Réseau Vrac et Réemploi to scale up cooperation within the reusable
management                      packaging sector and its transition to scale. This inter‑stakeholder cooperation will result in
                                widespread implementation of reusable packaging.
Deforestation and land‑use      In 2025, Carrefour signed an agreement with the government of the State of Para (Brazil),
change                          slaughterhouses and other industry players to set up a sustainable livestock breeding programme.
                                The aim is to guarantee individual traceability of all Para livestock by 2026, from birth to slaughter, in
                                order to prevent illegal deforestation linked to animal farming.
Microplastic emissions          Carrefour has made a commitment to reduce the use of virgin plastic in its own‑brand packaging.                    4
                                This reduction will be achieved through visible changes for consumers, such as deposits on reusable
                                packaging, eliminating plastic or including recycled plastic in packaging.
Consumption of energy           In June 2025, Carrefour signed a long‑term PPA (Power Purchase Agreement) with SUEZ under
resources                       which SUEZ will supply renewable electricity to Carrefour in France, produced by waste‑to‑energy
                                conversion. The contract covers around 700 GWh of renewable electricity.
Emissions of pollutants        For the first year, Carrefour Global Sourcing evaluated its suppliers via the Higg platform, which
impacting living organisms and integrates the management of chemicals, water and CO2 emissions.
food resources
                                                                                                                                                   5
Water consumption               Carrefour Spain, one of the Group’s countries identified as being the most sensitive to water stress,
                                has implemented a pilot action plan to support Carrefour in a more comprehensive approach to
                                water issues. The action plan includes the mapping of CQL supplier risks, training for all
                                Carrefour‑brand suppliers and the drafting of best practices to achieve water savings.
Risk of human rights violations
Inadequate working conditions In 2025, the Group rolled out its Supplier Ethics Charter, which now applies to suppliers of both
                              Carrefour brands and national brands. This charter draws on the following reference framework:
                                                                                                                                                   6
Forced labour                 ■ the Universal Declaration of Human Rights;
                              ■ the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights;
                              ■ the fundamental conventions of the International Labour Organization (ILO); and
Illegal work
                              ■ the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.

Failure to pay adequate wages Chapter 1 of the Charter covers human rights and working conditions and therefore addresses the
                              issues of forced labour, human trafficking and adequate wages.
Specific rights of indigenous   Carrefour Brazil has joined a scheme to support traditional communities via the Selo Origens label/
peoples                         initiative. This label aims to guarantee the origin and traceability of products from traditional forests          7
                                or territories, while supporting the inclusion of these communities in sustainable trade channels. An
                                investment fund has been allocated to support projects linked to these communities, including the
                                protection of forests, sustainable development, biodiversity and the local economy.
Unequal treatment and           Carrefour has signed a new Gender Equality and Diversity Agreement for 2025, aimed at
discrimination                  consolidating gender equality and diversity within the Group.
Risks to the health and safety of people
Occupational health and safety The aforementioned Supplier Ethics Charter also requires suppliers to respect the health and safety                 8
violations                     of their workers.

      2.2.8.3 Review of alerts received in 2025

                           MANIFESTATION
                                                                  ADDITIONAL MEASURES IN 2025 AND CONSOLIDATION OF
      RISKS COVERED        OF RISK OR ALERTS DATE
                                                                  EXISTING ACTION PLANS
                           IDENTIFIED IN 2025
      Consumption of       Sustainable fishing   March 2025       In March 2025, following two formal notices, Bloom and
      marine resources                                            Foodwatch took Carrefour to court over its procurement of fish,
                                                                  specifically tuna. Carrefour has implemented action plans on
                                                                  environmental issues, human rights, and individual health and
                                                                  safety. These action plans have already given rise to practical
                                                                  measures (updating the Supplier Ethics Charter; improving the
                                                                  sustainability of own‑brand stocks on offer, depending on the
                                                                  status of the species; improving risk mapping; etc.) and they are
                                                                  still being rolled out.
                                                                  Carrefour would also like to point out that the legal proceedings
                                                                  have in no way interrupted the implementation of these action
                                                                  plans.
      Deforestation and    Deforestation         September 2025   One of the world's largest wetlands, the Pantanal in Brazil, is
      land‑use change                                             believed to have been partially deforested using Agent Orange, an
                                                                  extremely toxic defoliant used by the USA during the Vietnam War.
                                                                  According to an investigation by the NGO Mighty Earth, some of
                                                                  the farms involved in this deforestation are supplied by JBS, a
                                                                  major player in the Brazilian agri‑food industry, and are indirectly
                                                                  linked to Carrefour.
                                                                  Carrefour would like to make it clear that no link has been
                                                                  established between the producer mentioned and that this
                                                                  producer has been proactively blocked since 2024. The Group
                                                                  would like to reiterate that its commitment to preventing all forms
                                                                  of deforestation does not depend on the technique used:
                                                                  Carrefour's policies and monitoring systems are designed to detect
                                                                  any conversion or loss of vegetation, whether as a result of
                                                                  mechanical clearing, fire, chemical degradation or other emerging
                                                                  practices.
                                                                  Current geomonitoring tools can already identify the first signs of
                                                                  degradation, even if the final change in land use may appear at a
                                                                  later date. Carrefour applies a strict protocol that includes weekly
                                                                  satellite tracking of all its suppliers, the automatic blocking of
                                                                  properties with evidence of deforestation or conversion, and
                                                                  cross‑checking alerts from PRODES, MapBiomas and fire‑detection
                                                                  systems to ensure that this type of deforestation does not enter its
                                                                  supply chain. Finally, any supplier involved in deforestation,
                                                                  whether chemical or otherwise, is automatically blocked, in line
                                                                  with Carrefour's deforestation policy, including JBS.

 Alexandre Bompard

CHAIRMAN AND CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER / Chairman of the Strategic Committee

                                       YEARS IN OFFICE: 8 YEARS                               ATTENDANCE RATE: 100%
                                                                                                                                                           2
                                       Alexandre Bompard is a graduate of Institut d'études politiques de Paris, with a degree in Public law and a
                                       postgraduate degree in Economics. He is also a graduate of École Nationale de l'Administration (ENA)
                                       (Cyrano de Bergerac class). After graduating from ENA, Alexandre Bompard joined the French General
                                       Inspectorate of Finance (1999‑2002). He went on to become the technical advisor to François Fillon,
                                       then Minister for Social Affairs, Labour and Solidarity (April‑December 2003). From 2004 to 2008, he held
BORN ON: October 4, 1972               several positions within the Canal+ group, notably as Chief of Staff for Chairman Bertrand Méheut

ALEXANDRE DE PALMAS

                       Alexandre de Palmas is a graduate of Institut d’Études Politiques de Paris and École Nationale de
                       l'Administration (ENA).
                       He began his career in retail property with the Casino group and subsequently held senior
                       management positions at Clear Channel, Gallimard‑Flammarion and then Elior. He joined the
                       Carrefour group in August 2018 as Executive Director, Convenience and cash & carry France. He             4
                       was appointed Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Carmila in July 2019.
                       In July 2020, he was appointed Executive Director of Carrefour Spain. In September 2023, he
                       became Executive Director, France.

HERVÉ DAUDIN

                       A former student of the École Normale Supérieure and engineer with the Corps des Ponts et
                       Chaussées, Hervé Daudin began his career at the Ministry of the Economy and Finance, before
                       joining the Casino group in 2002.
                       He was initially Director of Strategy and Planning, before taking on responsibilities in upstream
                       functions (logistics, supply, IT). Since 2009, he has been Merchandise Director, President of AMC
                       (the Casino Group central purchasing office) and member of the Executive Committee.
                       Hervé Daudin was appointed Group Executive Director, Merchandise on November 4, 2024.
                                                                                                                                 6

                       where she held various sales and marketing positions.

                       In 2015, she was appointed International Food Executive Officer at Intermarché.
                       Caroline Dassié joined Carrefour France in 2018 as Executive Director of Supermarkets, then as
                       Executive Director of Marketing and Clients for the Carrefour group from September 1, 2021.

                                      South‑Korea.

                                      France. In 2011, he joined the Fnac group as Chief Financial Officer and on July 20, 2016, following
                                      the company's acquisition of Darty, he became Chief Financial Officer of Fnac Darty.
                                      On October 16, 2017, Matthieu Malige took up the position of Chief Financial Officer of the
                                      Carrefour group.

PABLO LORENZO

                    Pablo Lorenzo holds a degree in accounting sciences from the National University of Lomas de
                    Zamora (UNLM) and a master's degree in finance from ESSEC Business School.
                    He joined the Carrefour group almost 30 years ago in Argentina, where he began his career as a
                    trainee. In Argentina, he held various management positions, including Director of Hypermarkets,
                    Director of Strategic Projects, Director of the Maxi format and Director of development of the
                    Express format.
                    In 2011, he joined the Executive Committee of Carrefour Argentina, where he became Managing                   2
                    Director in 2021. He led the digital transformation and the recovery in commercial activity in the
                    country. Pablo has also worked in Carrefour's Operations department in France and in the Finance
                    department, and in Spain as Director of Management Control and Director of Organisation.
                    In October 2023, he became COO of the Carrefour Brazil group, responsible for the operations of
                    Atacadão, Carrefour and Sam's Club. During this period, he implemented strategic initiatives such as
                    the 555 customer service model.
                    Since July 2025, Pablo has been Managing Director of the Carrefour Brazil group, Executive Director
                    for Latin America and a member of the Carrefour group Executive Committee.                                    3

JÉRÔME NANTY

                    Jérôme Nanty is a graduate of Institut d’Études Politiques de Paris and has a Master’s degree in
                    public law.
                    He began his career in 1986 at Société Générale before joining the capital markets division of Crédit
                    Lyonnais bank in 1989, first as a bond market operator and subsequently as a manager of a portfolio
                    of bond issuers. In 1998, he joined the bank's Human Resources department as manager of                       4
                    employment policy and later labour relations. From 2001 to 2004, he served as Director of Labour
                    and Social Relations for the Crédit Lyonnais group. From 2003 onwards, he held the same position
                    at the Crédit Agricole group. As such, he was in charge of the labour aspect of the merger of Crédit
                    Lyonnais and Crédit Agricole. He was appointed as Director of Human Resources at LCL in 2005
                    and at the Caisse des Dépôts group in 2008. From 2013 to 2016, he was General Secretary of the
                    Transdev group. Since July 2016, he has served as General Secretary and Director of Human
                    Resources of the Air France‑KLM group.
                    On October 2, 2017, Jérôme Nanty joined the Carrefour group as Executive Director, Human
                    Resources for the Group and France. In June 2019 he was appointed Executive Director, Human
                                                                                                                                  5
                    Resources and Assets for the Group and France.

      4.1 2025 risk management (1)

      In a constantly changing environment, risk management is                         to preventive or corrective measures designed to protect the
      essential to ensuring the long‑term viability of the Group’s                     Group’s value and reputation (4.1.1).
      business operations. A risk is the possibility that an event may
      occur and impact Carrefour’s strategy, assets and reputation, as                 The Group’s key risks in 2025, within the universe of 54 risks at
